primitives.name: Signal Acquisition Parallelization
primitives.verbatim_quote: Many operations in a GNSS receiver including but not limited to signal acquisition and tracking are inherently independent of each other and are run in parallel when a standard receiver is implemented in hardware [10].
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'N_{\\text{cores}}': 'number of CPU cores', 'T_{\\text{acq}}': 'acquisition time in seconds', 'S_{\\text{data}}': 'sampled data size in bits'}
primitives.assumptions: Operations are computationally independent; parallel execution does not introduce synchronization overhead.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When N_cores exceeds optimal thread count, diminishing returns occur due to memory contention.

layer2.mapping: Acquisition tasks map to independent threads in GSE, with GSI treating each as a probabilistic event under Bayesian framework.
layer2.telemetry: Measured via reduction in T_acq and increase in N_requests/sec.

primitives.name: Multi-Core Utilization
primitives.verbatim_quote: We describe the speedups we obtained by enabling the software to exploit multi-core CPUs and GPGPUs.
primitives.latex: \text{Speedup} = \frac{T_1}{T_p} \quad \text{where } T_1 \text{ is serial time, } T_p \text{ is parallel time}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'T_1': 'execution time with one core in seconds', 'T_p': 'execution time with p cores in seconds', 'p': 'number of cores used'}
primitives.assumptions: Task decomposition allows perfect load balancing across cores.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Performance saturates when memory bandwidth becomes bottleneck.

layer2.mapping: GSE uses multi-core scheduling kernel to distribute workload; GSI applies kernel density estimation to model task distribution.
layer2.telemetry: Observed speedup ratio against theoretical Amdahl’s law limits.

primitives.name: Effective Running Time
primitives.verbatim_quote: We use the notion of effective running time to measure the system's throughput when running multiple instances at the same time, and show how we can determine when the system's computing resources have been saturated.
primitives.latex: T_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_i \cdot w_i \quad \text{with } w_i \text{ being weight factor}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'T_{\\text{eff}}': 'effective running time in seconds', 't_i': 'individual task runtime in seconds', 'w_i': 'weighting coefficient for task i'}
primitives.assumptions: Tasks are weighted based on computational intensity and priority.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Resource saturation occurs when T_eff > total available compute time.

layer2.mapping: GSE tracks T_eff to manage concurrency limits; GSI uses it to estimate posterior confidence intervals.
layer2.telemetry: Throughput measured as number of completed requests per second.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that software GNSS receivers must balance latency and throughput in a cloud environment. Signal acquisition and tracking are naturally parallelizable, enabling multi-core and GPGPU acceleration. The system's performance hinges on minimizing synchronization overhead and maximizing data reuse. Effective running time quantifies how efficiently resources are used under concurrent loads. As more client requests arrive, the system scales by distributing workloads across cores, but eventually hits saturation due to shared memory or I/O bottlenecks. This leads to a trade-off between response time (per-request latency) and total throughput (requests/second). The mathematical formulation of speedup via Amdahl’s Law supports the empirical observation of diminishing returns beyond optimal core counts. Parallelism is modeled as a function of task independence and resource contention, where each acquisition channel operates independently until interference arises from shared memory access patterns.
